deptClusters.verification_notes: All eleven distinct sources opened successfully. Core vendor claims (550%, 200 hours, ISO 42001, 98%/70% figures, CORTEX_USER granted to PUBLIC, Cortex no-training, NIST AI 600-1, Power BI geographic and SKU restrictions, Foundry governance, Purview AI app coverage) were confirmed on the cited pages. Several details were overstated or unsupported and were softened or removed, most notably the Genie Code rename, KQL, one-click policies and the Purview investigation scenario. Figures remain vendor-reported, and regulatory hooks other than NIST remain unverified, so confidence stays medium. Re-research of departments 52, 53 (second pass): All four cited pages opened and broadly support the use cases; WIPO figures, the Körber platform list and the Equal Experts guardrails and 'dozens of ADRs in a morning' match the sources. Corrections were mostly overstated or unsupported wording and unverified vendor claims. Only the two cited sources per department were opened, so tool-fit statements about other products remain unverified; confidence stays medium.

deptClusters.cluster_overview: Research for this cluster is incomplete. Only two vendor pages (Atlassian Jira AI and UiPath Autopilot) were opened and both were re-opened and checked in verification. Other attempts failed (PMI returned 403; ServiceNow and McKinsey pages failed; the Microsoft and SAP pages held no usable product content). Every department therefore has at most one opened source, below the two-source target, and all are low confidence. Statements marked "not verified" come from general practice, not from an opened page. The expected shared pattern is that all seven departments turn semi-structured operational records (tickets, status updates, SOPs, audit findings, incident logs) into summaries, drafts and exception lists. The shared risks are confidential project, supplier and incident data, personal data in tickets and change feedback (GDPR), and unreviewed AI output entering formal records (SLAs, quality records, recovery plans). Suggested joint training is a shared module on process and ticket data hygiene and human review of AI outputs. Joint sessions are also suggested for 55/56/58 (process and SOP work), 54/57 (portfolio and change reporting), and 59 with 55 (incident communications). All of this needs verification before it goes into the handbook. A follow-up with fresh search budget is recommended.

departments.name: Project & Program Management Office
ai_use_cases: Drafting project status updates from Rovo chat in Jira (Rovo Project Management skills: create work items, update work items, draft status updates). [1]
Summarising a Jira work item's status, contributors, next steps, blockers and recent updates for fast catch-up. [1]
Breaking work down into manageable tasks with summaries and descriptions via Rovo's work breakdown. [1]
Checking that work is clear and complete before planning via a 'Work Readiness Checker' agent, which Atlassian says reduces wasted work and follow-up meetings (vendor claim). [1]
Dependency and risk summaries from exported plans using a general LLM: not verified.
departments.capstone_deliverable: A weekly portfolio status pack for a real or realistic 3-project portfolio. It contains an AI-drafted status report per project, a dependency and risk summary, and a one-page executive view. Each project's figures are validated against the source tracker. The deliverable includes a documented prompt library and a measured time-saved log (baseline versus AI-assisted). Core-tier hours.
departments.data_risks: Project plans, budgets, vendor contracts and unannounced strategic initiatives are confidential. Resource data (names, utilisation) is personal data under GDPR and employment law. Rules: use only the enterprise-licensed assistant, exclude M&A or other MNPI-bearing projects from non-approved tools, and have a human owner verify every figure before it reaches a steering committee. The Atlassian page states privacy-by-design and that organisation admins can deactivate AI [1]; contractual data terms are not verified.
departments.adoption_kpis: Percentage of status reports AI-assisted; hours to produce the weekly report (baseline versus now); report factual-error rate found on review; share of PMs trained and active weekly; reduction in status meetings or follow-up queries.

departments.name: Service Delivery & Managed Services
ai_use_cases: A virtual service agent handles tier-one requests such as password resets and software access, deflecting tickets; Thumbtack reports 15% of requests handled without human involvement and SLA compliance raised from 90% to 95% on Jira Service Management (customer case study, vendor-published) [1].
The virtual agent gathers initial details so tickets arrive pre-populated, and offers 24/7 availability (home-services IT director interviewed in a Forrester TEI study) [2].
Agent-assist features: issue summarisation, response generation, sentiment analysis and recommended actions to cut handling effort [2].
AIOps-style support for incident and change management to make better-informed decisions [2].
Intent and template suggestions generated from historical request data to speed service-desk setup and expose service gaps [2].
Not verified: ServiceNow Now Assist case summaries and resolution notes (documentation pages did not load).
departments.capstone_deliverable: A monthly SLA and incident-pattern report for one real (anonymised) queue: AI-drafted narrative, a table of the top 5 recurring incident themes, and 3 proposed knowledge articles. Includes a validation log checking every figure against the source export, the documented prompts, and measured time saved versus the manual report (Advanced tier hours).
departments.data_risks: Tickets contain employee and customer personal data (GDPR), credentials or system details pasted by users, and contractual SLA and pricing terms. Rules: use only the approved in-platform or enterprise AI, strip personal data and secrets before pasting elsewhere, never share client-confidential data across client tenants, and have a human verify SLA figures before they go into customer reports. Forrester interviewees noted AI quality depends on knowledge content, so keep articles current [2].
departments.adoption_kpis: Virtual-agent deflection or auto-resolution rate; SLA compliance percentage; agent handling time per ticket; share of tickets with AI-assisted summary accepted unedited; knowledge articles created or refreshed per month.
departments.curriculum_emphasis: Spend most hours on hands-on work with the service platform's embedded AI (ServiceNow Now Assist where ServiceNow is the platform) for summarisation and knowledge, then Power BI Copilot for SLA reporting, and Claude or Gemini for incident-pattern analysis on exported, anonymised data. Prioritise verification habits, since automation outcomes depend on data and knowledge quality.
departments.tool_fit_commentary: ServiceNow Now Assist fits where ServiceNow is the ITSM platform, but the opened evidence is for Jira Service Management, which the handbook omits for this department [1][2]. Jira Service Management's AI is used for service desks (Thumbtack, Forrester TEI study; both vendor-commissioned or vendor-published). Ensure the training covers whichever ITSM platform the learner actually uses. Microsoft 365 Copilot and Gemini are general-purpose and not evidenced by these sources.

departments.name: Business Operations & Process Excellence
ai_use_cases: Turning plain-language descriptions into working automations in UiPath Studio via Autopilot, with the vendor claiming 50% faster delivery (vendor claim). [1]
Capturing workflows from live systems and translating business requirements into BPMN designs (Autopilot in Maestro) for process mapping. [1]
Generating tests from requirements and analysing results to keep automation quality high. [1]
Monitoring queues and schedules, surfacing failures early and resolving incidents in plain language. [1]
SOP drafting from process maps or recordings with an LLM: not verified.
departments.capstone_deliverable: One end-to-end process improvement package. It contains an AS-IS process map, an AI-assisted TO-BE design, a draft SOP reviewed against actual practice by a process owner, and an automation or workflow specification. The package includes a documented prompt log and a measured cycle-time or effort estimate. Advanced-tier hours.
departments.data_risks: Process documentation exposes internal controls (relevant to SOX where financial processes are mapped), customer or employee data in sample records, and credentials in recordings. Rules: use synthetic or masked data in prompts, route automations through governed platforms, and require owner sign-off on SOPs. UiPath states Autopilot actions can be recorded through the AI Trust Layer in a GDPR-compliant manner and that Autopilot uses only admin-approved tools [1]; this is a vendor statement, not a compliance guarantee.
departments.adoption_kpis: Number of processes mapped or documented per quarter; SOP drafting time; automations delivered per builder; rework rate of AI-drafted SOPs; percentage of automations built with governed AI assistance.
departments.curriculum_emphasis: Prioritise UiPath Autopilot and Power Automate (build and governance), Claude (process analysis, SOP writing), and Microsoft 365 Copilot (document and meeting capture). Emphasise validation of AI-drawn maps against observed work.
departments.tool_fit_commentary: Good fit; UiPath Autopilot is confirmed as an assistant for building, operating and troubleshooting automations [1]. Gamma is a weak fit (presentation, not process work). Omissions not verified: process-mining and mapping tools (for example Celonis, Signavio); the UiPath page itself lists Process Intelligence and Maestro as related products [1].

Drafting key change messages and tailoring communications to different audiences [1].
Developing resistance-management tactics for a given initiative [1].

departments.name: Quality Management & Process Compliance
ai_use_cases: Generate a narrative summary of a deviation investigation or CAPA plan from related Investigation, Root Cause and CAPA Action records (Veeva Vault QMS Deviation Agent, in Vaults using Vault AI for Quality); the user reviews and saves it [1].
Answer questions about a deviation record through an in-product AI chat [1].
Surface similar past deviations and shared factors to support root-cause analysis; the quality engineer stays in control (vendor article) [3].

AI-supported CAPA and deviation work under human accountability; a consultancy blog summarises the draft EU Annex 22 as requiring transparency, model validation and continuous performance monitoring, and Annex 11 as extending validation, access control and audit trail to AI-enabled systems [2]. Not verified: that draft Annex 22 covers generative drafting of CAPA content.
Not verified: quantified time savings for any of these.
departments.capstone_deliverable: A quality audit summary and root-cause analysis for a de-identified deviation or audit finding set: AI-drafted summary, 5-Whys or fishbone, proposed SOP changes, and a human review log showing every AI statement checked against records. Includes documented prompts and time saved.
departments.data_risks: Quality records are GxP or regulated records with batch, patient-safety, supplier and audit data; in pharma, data integrity and Annex 11 or 21 CFR Part 11-type controls apply, and complaints may carry personal or health data (GDPR, HIPAA). departments.adoption_kpis: Time to draft investigation or CAPA summaries; share of AI drafts accepted after review; CAPA cycle time; recurrence rate of similar deviations; audit findings on AI-assisted records.
departments.curriculum_emphasis: Emphasise review discipline and traceability over generation. Prioritise Claude for document summarisation and root-cause structuring on de-identified inputs, Microsoft 365 Copilot for SOP drafting, and Power BI Copilot for quality trend views. Cover validation expectations.
departments.tool_fit_commentary: The handbook list is general-purpose and omits the embedded QMS AI that quality teams actually use, such as Veeva Vault QMS's Deviation Agent [1]; MasterControl was not verified. Gamma is a weak fit for controlled quality records. Validation and audit-trail expectations for AI in GxP systems [2] make general chat tools hard to justify for regulated records; confirm the current status and scope of Annex 22 with a primary source before teaching it.

departments.name: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery

AI helps identify critical risks, assess impact, propose mitigation and simulate scenarios (Riskonnect, stated as ongoing integration) [1].
Natural-language prompts to create, refine and maintain incident response plans (AlertMedia AI Plan Builder) [3].
AI support for creating and sending critical messages during events, with human judgment kept central (Everbridge) [4].

Use AI to keep plans current: Forrester/DRJ 2026 data show about 59% update DR plans annually and only 32% have a recovery-readiness dashboard, which indicates room for assisted maintenance (my inference) [2].
departments.capstone_deliverable: A recovery playbook and tabletop-exercise pack for one scenario (for example a ransomware outage of one critical service): AI-drafted playbook, injects, and holding statements, checked against the real BIA and RTO/RPO. Includes documented prompts, review sign-off, and time saved (Specialist tier hours).
departments.data_risks: BCM files hold critical-system architecture, RTO/RPO, supplier dependencies, crisis contact lists (personal data, GDPR) and emergency notification content. Rules: treat plans as confidential security material, no real credentials or network diagrams in public models, validate all AI-generated recovery steps by exercise, and have Legal and Communications approve external or regulator-facing messages.
departments.adoption_kpis: Time to draft or refresh a plan; percentage of plans reviewed within cycle; exercise completion rate and issues found; time to issue first incident communication; share of critical services with a readiness dashboard.
departments.curriculum_emphasis: Focus on scenario and exercise design with Claude or ChatGPT Enterprise, plan drafting inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, and ServiceNow Now Assist only where BCM runs on that platform. Emphasise validation by testing, since fewer than 40% of respondents felt very or extremely prepared for a site failure or disaster [2].
departments.tool_fit_commentary: The handbook list is generic. It omits purpose-built BCM and crisis tools with AI: Riskonnect [1], AlertMedia [3] and Everbridge [4]; Fusion Risk Management was only seen in search results (not verified). ServiceNow Now Assist is a reasonable fit for IT-led DR but no opened source demonstrates it for this function.

departments.data_risks: Supply chain data covers supplier pricing and contract terms (commercial confidentiality, antitrust sensitivity), customer demand forecasts, and, for public companies, forward-looking volume data that can be material non-public information. Rules: keep ERP extracts within approved tools, anonymise suppliers when using general chat tools, verify AI-calculated quantities before ordering, and keep a human decision-maker for commitments.
departments.adoption_kpis: Planner time per exception; forecast accuracy and bias; stock-out and excess-inventory rates; share of exceptions resolved within target time; supplier on-time-in-full reporting cycle time.
departments.curriculum_emphasis: Prioritise SAP Joule (if SAP is the planning system) for exception analysis, Power BI Copilot for inventory and supplier dashboards, and Claude or Gemini for analysing exported data and drafting supplier communications. Stress checking calculations and assumptions.
departments.tool_fit_commentary: SAP Joule fits SAP IBP users, but it is irrelevant to firms on other planning platforms [1]. The handbook omits dedicated planning platforms such as Kinaxis, o9 and Blue Yonder, which appeared in searches but were not opened (not verified). Gartner's survey shows agentic AI adoption across the supply chain, which the list does not address [2].

runs.overview: The handbook covers security assistants (Security Copilot, Charlotte AI, Gemini in Security, Purview) and two observability tools (Datadog, Dynatrace), but names no SIEM or SecOps platform (Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk, Cortex XSIAM) and no open-stack observability platform (Grafana Cloud), though all appear in the 2025 Gartner SIEM or Observability Magic Quadrants. runs.verification_notes: All cited pages were opened and the core adoption claims (Gartner MQ placements, Sentinel 25,000 organizations, XSIAM $1B bookings, Vertex rebrand and named customers) matched the text. Most evidence is vendor-authored, with independent confirmation only for Sentinel and the Google platform, so medium confidence is the honest ceiling for Splunk, Cortex XSIAM, Grafana and Dataiku. Unsupported details were dropped (Splunk Observability MQ and AI Assistant specifics, XSIAM FedRAMP High) and SageMaker Unified Studio was removed for lack of verified adoption evidence. Fabric is retained at low confidence only because its evidence is thin and it partly overlaps Power BI Copilot.

Corrected Microsoft Sentinel: confidence raised to high because Virtualization Review independently confirms 25,000 organizations and Gartner and Forrester Leader placements.

Corrected Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: confidence raised to high; clarified that the Gartner DSML Leader ranking was earned as Vertex AI; added verified Tata Steel and GE Appliances (800+ agents) details; Google blog dated 5 Jun 2025.

runs.overview: The 60 departments cover governance, finance, HR, go-to-market, technology and operations well, but miss several external-facing and workplace shared services that large companies staff separately. All five candidates are absent from the 60 and none is a renamed duplicate. Executive Administration overlaps most with the Office of the CEO and Workplace Administration. Near-misses left out as not verified: internal communications, sales enablement, legal operations, knowledge management, physical security, events and localisation.

candidates.name: Corporate Communications & Public Relations
candidates.why_missing: No listed department owns media relations, reputation, executive messaging and crisis communications; Marketing & Brand and the Office of the CEO touch it only partly.
candidates.typical_org_types: All large companies, especially listed, consumer-facing and regulated firms.
candidates.workplace_application: Drafting press releases and executive statements, media and sentiment monitoring, crisis Q&A preparation.
candidates.ai_use_evidence: Opened: a Wadds Inc. management briefing lists AI use cases in corporate communications and PR (content creation, brainstorming, research, media pitching) and flags risks of unauthorised AI use. Opened: USC Annenberg's 2025 Relevance Report (published 30 Dec 2024), curated with Microsoft, gathers views of over 40 communications leaders on using AI in daily team work. Both pages are descriptive summaries, not adoption statistics.
candidates.data_risks: Unreleased announcements, market-sensitive information, embargoed material and crisis plans.

sources.title: The Use of AI in Corporate Communications and Public Relations: The Story So Far (Wadds Inc.)
Study reveals rising application of AI across communications by the public relations industry (USC)

candidates.name: Government Affairs & Public Policy
candidates.why_missing: Legislative tracking, lobbying, advocacy and regulator engagement are not covered; Regulatory Compliance handles obligations, not influence.
candidates.typical_org_types: Regulated and policy-exposed industries: financial services, energy, healthcare, tech, telecoms, defence.
candidates.workplace_application: Bill and regulation monitoring, one-page legislative briefs, tailored stakeholder outreach drafts.
candidates.ai_use_evidence: Opened (Sept 2026): the Public Affairs Council 2026 benchmarking report finds 99% of surveyed organisations use AI, 73% have an organisation-wide AI policy (up from 33% in 2024) and 81% cite efficiency gains; only 7% say AI is embedded in strategic decision-making. Opened: Quorum's blog (vendor source) cites its 2025 survey of 200-plus government affairs professionals and describes AI bill analysis, hearing summaries and drafting with ChatGPT. The earlier claim of '54% of teams deploy AI' was not found on the opened page and is dropped.
candidates.data_risks: Confidential policy positions, stakeholder and legislator relationship data, and political contribution records.

sources.title: From Experimentation to Everyday Use: New Council Research on AI in Public Affairs
Top Challenges in Government Affairs in 2025 (and How AI Can Help) - Quorum

candidates.name: Corporate Real Estate & Workplace Strategy
candidates.why_missing: Portfolio, lease and space-planning decisions are not owned by Workplace Administration & Facilities, which covers day-to-day operations.
candidates.typical_org_types: Large office-based and multi-site companies; asset-heavy sectors such as retail, banking and pharma.

Opened: JLL's 2026 benchmark (via Allwork.Space, 20 May 2026) finds over 70% still researching or not started AI in occupancy planning, privacy the top barrier at 70%, and Power BI the most used analytics platform. runs.verification_notes: All nine cited pages opened and support AI use in the relevant function, but several are summaries or vendor-sponsored (Quorum, Vimcal, Wadds), so evidence strength varies. Government Affairs and Pricing rest on solid survey data (Public Affairs Council, McKinsey). Executive Administration is the weakest: no figures on the ASAP page, only second-hand numbers via a vendor newsletter, and some overlap with existing departments. No candidate is a duplicate of the 60; recommended tools are real products and fit.
removed_or_corrected: Government Affairs: removed the unsupported 'Quorum 2025 survey reports 54% of teams deploy AI' claim; the opened Quorum page does not show it. Replaced with what the page does say.
Government Affairs: added that the Council's 73% policy figure was up from 33% in 2024 and that only 7% embed AI in strategic decisions, for balance.
Corporate Real Estate: confidence lowered from high to medium; the 78% figure is Asia Pacific only, and JLL shows over 70% have not moved beyond research on AI in occupancy planning.
Pricing & Revenue Management: McKinsey article dated 7 April 2026 and the 10-30% figure clarified as current adoption; confidence kept at medium (single source).

Executive Administration: ASAP page gives no figures; the numbers (26% AI use, 86% ChatGPT) come from the Vimcal newsletter citing ASAP's 2024 report; overlap with Office of the CEO and Workplace Administration noted; confidence kept low.
Corporate Communications: clarified that sources are descriptive and give no adoption statistics; USC report is dated 30 Dec 2024.

runs.overview: The 60 departments cover corporate, commercial, technology and support functions but omit line-of-business functions: plants, laboratories, field crews, stores, claims desks and fraud operations. Checks found no candidate that duplicates an existing department, though Quality Control Laboratory Operations and Manufacturing Operations sit closest to Quality Management (58) and Supply Chain (60). All nine candidates have at least one opened page showing AI use, but most evidence is vendor, analyst or trade-press material with self-reported figures. Grid & Network Operations and Quality Control Laboratory Operations are the weakest, since each rests largely on a session abstract or a vendor article.

candidates.name: Manufacturing Operations & Plant Maintenance
candidates.why_missing: Production, plant maintenance and reliability engineering are not covered by Supply Chain (60) or Quality Management (58), which focus on flow and compliance rather than machine uptime and shop-floor work.
candidates.typical_org_types: Manufacturers, process industries, food, automotive, energy and chemicals
candidates.workplace_application: Summarising machine fault history and manuals, drafting maintenance work orders and shift handovers, analysing downtime and failure patterns
candidates.ai_use_evidence: Plant Services' January 2026 roundup lists AI maintenance case studies, including Fiberon avoiding $274,000 in costs and 178 downtime hours in an AI pilot, and KONE achieving 70% more proactive fault detection [1]. Siemens Industrial Copilot has been piloted with Schaeffler, helping automation engineers and OT staff with repetitive tasks and code generation [2]. The Siemens/Schaeffler article describes engineering and automation use more than shop-floor troubleshooting.
candidates.data_risks: Plant sensor data, equipment configurations and process recipes are trade secrets, and connected operational technology adds safety and cyber exposure.

sources.title: Top 5 predictive maintenance case studies from Plant Services in 2025
With Industrial Copilot, Siemens and Schaeffler help make Gen-AI industrial grade

candidates.name: Insurance Underwriting & Claims
candidates.why_missing: Risk selection, policy pricing and claims adjudication are core insurer functions; Enterprise Risk Management (5) and Customer Support (37) do not cover them.
candidates.typical_org_types: Insurers, reinsurers, brokers and claims administrators
candidates.workplace_application: Summarising broker submissions and claim files, checking completeness against underwriting guidelines, drafting claimant and policy correspondence
candidates.ai_use_evidence: Celent's July 2025 post cites a survey of 55 insurers with 44% having active genAI deployments as of May 2025, QBE's cyber underwriting assistant reading and summarising submissions, and Zurich's ZuriChat suggesting policy phrasing and checking decisions against guidelines [1]. Allianz's Insurance Copilot, launched in 2024 for motor claims in Austria, lets adjusters ask questions of claim data [2].
candidates.data_risks: Claimant health, financial and incident data plus pricing models are regulated personal data, and automated decisions raise fairness and explainability obligations.

sources.title: Celent: What the Evolution of GenAI in Underwriting Says about the Future of GenAI in Insurance
Allianz: Smarter claims management, smoother settlements

candidates.name: Payments Fraud & Credit Risk Operations
candidates.why_missing: Transaction fraud monitoring and credit decisioning are not covered by Enterprise Risk Management (5) or Cybersecurity Operations (47); AML policy sits in Regulatory Compliance (7). Opened evidence covers fraud only; the credit risk part is not verified.
candidates.typical_org_types: Banks, card networks, fintechs, lenders and large retailers with credit programmes
candidates.workplace_application: Summarising fraud alerts and case evidence, drafting suspicious-activity narratives, analysing false-positive patterns in rules and models

runs.verification_notes: Every cited page opened, and each candidate has at least one opened page showing AI use in its function; none duplicates an existing department. Several specific figures were checked against the opened text (Fiberon, KONE, Celent 44%, Mastercard, PTC, Siemens 10,000 technicians, Passport 6,483, Bain). The Freyr 30% and 70% figures could not be found and were dropped. Most evidence is vendor, analyst or trade press with self-reported outcomes; Grid & Network Operations and Quality Control Laboratory Operations are weakest and are rated low. Tool lists were not independently verified beyond the cited products (ServiceMax AI, Siemens Industrial Copilot, Copilot for Dynamics 365).
removed_or_corrected: Clinical & Regulatory Affairs: removed the Freyr 30% cycle-time and 70% effort-reduction claims and its source citation because the figures were not found in the opened page; kept Kanda only.
Clinical & Regulatory Affairs: removed the tool 'Veeva Vault RIM AI' as unverified.
Field Service & Technician Operations: replaced 'Microsoft Teams Copilot' with 'Microsoft Copilot for Dynamics 365 Field Service', which the opened Microsoft Siemens page supports.
Grid & Network Operations: removed 'Datadog Bits AI' as an IT observability tool that does not fit control-room work; T&D World source now noted as not supporting control-room use.
Manufacturing Operations & Plant Maintenance: corrected the Siemens/Schaeffler description, since the opened article covers engineering and OT assistance rather than shop-floor troubleshooting.
Insurance Underwriting & Claims: corrected the Allianz description and Zurich/QBE details to match the opened pages.
Payments Fraud & Credit Risk Operations: noted the Mastercard evidence is network-level fraud detection.

candidates.name: AI Governance & Responsible AI Office
candidates.why_missing: Department 5 covers enterprise risk and 48 covers security and privacy, but neither owns AI use-case intake, AI risk review boards or responsible-AI policy. Department 51 builds AI and does not govern it.
candidates.typical_org_types: All large companies, especially financial services, insurance, healthcare and the public sector.
candidates.workplace_application: Triage AI use-case intake requests, draft risk-assessment rationale against policy frameworks, summarise AI board papers and decisions.
candidates.ai_use_evidence: A large insurer with a backlog of over 100 AI use-case review requests redesigned its AI risk review intake and workflow, shortening average review-to-closure times [1]. This is evidence of AI governance work itself; the opened page does not show AI being used to automate the reviews. A Gartner poll found 55% of organisations have an AI board and 54% have a head of AI [2].
candidates.data_risks: Inventories of AI systems, model risk ratings, vendor contracts and internal policy decisions that are confidential and can be regulator-relevant.

sources.title: Insurer streamlines AI governance to manage risk and spur innovation (Grant Thornton)
Gartner: 55% of Firms Now Rely on AI Governance Boards (BankInfoSecurity)

candidates.name: Model Risk Management & Validation
candidates.why_missing: Department 5 covers enterprise risk in general, but no department owns independent model validation, the model inventory or the new testing needed for generative AI. Department 51 builds models. Partial overlap with 5 is possible, hence Specialist tier.
candidates.typical_org_types: Banks, insurers, asset managers, lenders and other regulated financial institutions.
candidates.workplace_application: Draft model validation reports, design hallucination and bias test plans, maintain model inventory documentation.
candidates.ai_use_evidence: A March 2025 arXiv paper by bank-affiliated authors outlines the extra model risk controls and validation practices large US banks need for generative AI, citing hallucinations and toxicity as the main new risks [1]. KPMG's page says traditional validation falls short for generative AI and describes tests for hallucinations and bias and how Gen AI fits into a validation framework [2]. Both show AI's impact on the function; neither is a case of the function using AI tools.
candidates.data_risks: Proprietary model code, validation findings, and customer and credit data used in testing, all subject to supervisory scrutiny.

sources.title: Model Risk Management for Generative AI In Financial Institutions (arXiv)
Gen AI transforming model validation in banking (KPMG)

candidates.name: Revenue Enablement

sources.title: 2025 AI in Revenue Enablement Report released (Allego)

runs.overview: The 60 departments cover risk, compliance, data engineering and AI/ML build work, but they have no home for the control and enablement layer that AI adoption created: the offices that approve AI use cases, validate AI models, steward the data that feeds them, and enable revenue teams to use AI. Near-misses are 5 Enterprise Risk Management, 48 Security Governance, Risk & Privacy and 51 AI, ML & Automation, which hold parts of these functions without owning them. Developer experience, customer insights, digital workplace and AI centres of excellence were judged folded into 43/44, 33, 45/18 and 51. A knowledge management function had only one opened source and was dropped.
runs.verification_notes: All cited pages except one were opened and support the stated claims, with minor corrections. The SalesTechStar page returned 403 and was dropped; the Allego page carries the same statistics. The Grant Thornton page does not show an AI-for-AI automation, so that claim was removed. Several sources describe AI's effect on a function or vendor survey data rather than documented deployments, so confidence is moderate at best for the validation, data governance and revenue enablement candidates. Tool names were not individually verified for these four candidates.
removed_or_corrected: AI Governance: removed the claim that the insurer explored an AI-for-AI capability to automate reviews; the opened Grant Thornton page shows only a redesigned intake, workflow and operating model with shorter review-to-closure times.
Model Risk Management: KPMG page covers hallucination and bias tests, not toxicity; toxicity attributed only to the arXiv abstract. Noted overlap with department 5.
Data Governance: AWS URL corrected to the trailing-slash form that opened; evidence reworded to match the ITL article (metadata generation, data quality rules, stewardship).
Revenue Enablement: removed the SalesTechStar source (HTTP 403, not opened); Allego page supports the statistics. Added survey size (346) and noted overlap risk with departments 30 and 13.
Overview: removed the unverified statement about APQC and Microsoft Inside Track pages (not cited either way).

merged.name: Model Risk Management & Validation
merged.why_missing: Department 5 covers enterprise risk in general, but no department owns independent model validation, the model inventory or the new testing needed for generative AI. Department 51 builds models. Partial overlap with 5 is possible, hence Specialist tier.
merged.typical_org_types: Banks, insurers, asset managers, lenders and other regulated financial institutions.
merged.workplace_application: Draft model validation reports, design hallucination and bias test plans, maintain model inventory documentation.
merged.ai_use_evidence: A March 2025 arXiv paper by bank-affiliated authors outlines the extra model risk controls and validation practices large US banks need for generative AI, citing hallucinations and toxicity as the main new risks [1]. KPMG's page says traditional validation falls short for generative AI and describes tests for hallucinations and bias and how Gen AI fits into a validation framework [2]. Both show AI's impact on the function; neither is a case of the function using AI tools.
merged.data_risks: Proprietary model code, validation findings, and customer and credit data used in testing, all subject to supervisory scrutiny.

sources.title: Model Risk Management for Generative AI In Financial Institutions (arXiv)
Gen AI transforming model validation in banking (KPMG)

merged.name: Data Governance & Stewardship
merged.why_missing: Department 49 builds data platforms and pipelines, and 48 covers privacy. Neither owns data ownership, catalogues, definitions, quality standards or steward roles.
merged.typical_org_types: All large companies, especially insurance, banking, healthcare and manufacturing.
merged.workplace_application: Draft business glossary definitions and missing metadata, write data quality rules, summarise lineage and policy exceptions.
merged.ai_use_evidence: AWS advises building a central data catalogue, appointing domain data quality stewards and automating quality checks to prepare data for generative AI [1]. An Insurance Thought Leadership article (Feb 2025) says generative AI can generate business-attribute metadata, including missing metadata for legacy systems, create data quality rules and streamline stewardship [2].
merged.data_risks: Personal data, customer and financial records and data lineage across systems, where mislabelled sensitivity classes cause leakage or compliance breaches.

sources.title: Data Governance in the Age of Generative AI (AWS)
AI Transforms P&C Insurance Data Governance (Insurance Thought Leadership)

merged.name: Revenue Enablement
merged.why_missing: Department 30 handles sales and revenue operations, and 13 handles learning and development. Neither owns sales content, rep onboarding, coaching and playbooks across sales, marketing and customer success. Some overlap with 30 and 13, so a duplicate risk remains.
merged.typical_org_types: B2B technology, financial services, life sciences and manufacturing companies with large sales forces.
merged.workplace_application: Generate sales decks and battlecards, run AI role-play coaching, build onboarding learning paths from call insights.
merged.ai_use_evidence: Allego's 2025 AI in Revenue Enablement Report, a survey of 346 B2B revenue enablement leaders, found 100% use generative AI, 81% use AI to create content such as sales presentations and emails (up from 28% in 2024), 60% use it for real-time feedback during sales calls, and 51% report shorter sales cycles and faster onboarding [1]. The survey is vendor-run and self-reported.
merged.data_risks: Customer call recordings, deal and pricing information and unreleased product messaging.

sources.title: 2025 AI in Revenue Enablement Report released (Allego)
